plan_budgets.overview: Let a plan with visual changes carry before-and-after screenshots into its design document, copied with the plan to the GitHub and Linear boards as image assets.
plan_budgets.sizing: A visual plan of 2 to 12 images (up to 24 in its largest first copy, about 500 KB each), copied 1 to 4 times, with up to 3 managers finishing plans at once on one shared board token.
plan_budgets.workload: A plan with visual changes has 1 to 6 expected visual changes, typically 2, so its `spike-visual-report` and its design document each hold 2 to 12 images (typically 4), each a PNG of 50 to 500 KB captured from a browser page or a rendered terminal. Such a plan is copied to its board once by `just finish-plan` and re-copied 1 to 3 more times as it is edited, so a first copy carries up to 24 new images and a re-copy usually none. On GitHub, a first copy of the largest visual plan sends about 49 content-creating requests: 24 uploads plus about 25 issue and board mutations for the plan's own records (project issue, about 7 task issues, 3 document issues and their board items). It also sends 24 verifying reads. This host plans 1 to 3 plans a day, about a third of them visual. **The burst that matters is concurrency**: up to 3 managers on this host may finish plans at once, sharing the `plans` board token and Hello Patient's Linear key. That makes about 147 content-creating requests to GitHub within a couple of minutes, against GitHub's published secondary limit of 80 content-creating requests a minute (and 500 an hour), which onetaskgraph's github-projects plugin paces one process at by default (one every 750 ms) and waits out for at most 120 s per call. Every check that counts or times image copies uses generated PNGs of that size, and every timed or rate-limited journey runs on a simulated clock, so the published limits are enforced in virtual time and no check sleeps for real: each between 50 KB and 500 KB (50,000 to 500,000 bytes), and for the largest plan 24 images of about 500 KB each (450,000 to 500,000 bytes), about 12 MB uploaded, hashed, stored and serialized per copy. Plans without visual change carry no asset at all. A visual plan also dispatches one `spike-visual`, capped at 40 turns by the manager's ruling (see spend).
plan_budgets.ten_x_summary: At 10 concurrent first copies, GitHub's secondary rate limiter refuses copies; accepted past 3 at once, which is budgeted.
plan_budgets.ten_x: The first user-visible failure is a copy refused by GitHub's secondary rate limiter on the shared `plans` token. That happens when several managers finish visual plans at once, not because of the per-image request count. At realistic concurrency (3 simultaneous first copies of 24-image plans, about 147 content-creating requests against 80 a minute) it is covered by `github-concurrent-copies-refused` (0 refused copies), with the wait it costs bounded by `github-concurrent-copy-seconds` (240 s for the slowest copy). Each plugin must pace uploads with its mutations and wait out a limiter refusal within its bounded retry budget for those to hold. At 10× (about 10 simultaneous copies, about 490 content-creating requests in one burst, near GitHub's 500-an-hour ceiling as well) no per-process pacing can avoid it: each call's 120 s retry budget runs out and copies are refused by name, naming the limiter. Copy latency is unbounded until the person re-runs the copy. That residual is not budgeted: the manager accepted throttling past the budgeted 3 concurrent first copies by ruling on exception 7, and a limiter shared across processes on the host, which covering it would need, is not planned.

checklist.not_applicable: n/a for a new budget. onetaskgraph has no gate-time budget, and ai-orchestrator's `gate-time` (1800 s) absorbs its few template tests and two journeys, which add a few seconds. For onetaskgraph, the asset journeys run once, in the ordinary `test` targets of `onetaskgraph-github-projects-e2e` and `onetaskgraph-linear-e2e`, and only when a change affects those domains. They add an estimated 10 to 30 s of real time to each of those test runs: generating about 110 noise PNGs (about 55 MB), passing them through the loopback, and spawning the binary. They never sleep for pacing, backoff or loopback latency, because those run on a simulated clock. Each node reports the figure it measured, and holds its three-process journey under 60 s of real time. The `budgets` targets add only telemetry analysis, well under a second per budget. They run no journey a second time and are cached on the domain tree, the measured production code and the onebudgetspec pin. The plan as first written would instead have re-run every journey for its budget and slept through about 6 to 10 minutes of real pacing and backoff per affected check.
checklist.summary: A few seconds of new tests, absorbed by the existing gate-time budget.

checklist.not_applicable: n/a because ai-orchestrator's `cycle-time` budget already measures each landed change, and this plan expects no effect on it beyond the chain's own release waits.
checklist.summary: The existing cycle-time budget already measures every landed change.

realistic_data.artifact: onetaskgraph's test-image generator in `crates/onetaskgraph-e2e-support` (added by otg-assets-core), used by the plugin domains' journeys, whose recorded telemetry the budgets analyse; ai-orchestrator's finish-plan and approve-design journeys generate theirs the same way. The positive planning-flow journey generates its disposable target's visual content in the test, sized so the real renderer's captures of it are each 50,000 to 500,000 bytes (at least one of about 500 KB), and asserts every capture's encoded size before copying it.
realistic_data.data: Screenshot images carried by a copy
realistic_data.reason: Real screenshots cannot be had before the feature exists, and a generated image of the same size exercises the same upload, hashing, storage and serialization as one. So each test generates PNGs of seeded pseudo-random pixels, which compression cannot shrink, distinct per image (one changed between copies), sized as real screenshots are: each 50 KB to 500 KB, and for the largest-plan measurements 24 images of about 500 KB each. Generating them costs well under a second, where committed fixture images of that size would add about 12 MB to a repository and need upkeep; they are never committed.
realistic_data.summary: Generated noise PNGs of 50 to 500 KB: real-sized uploads with nothing to commit or maintain.

budgets.inner_measure_reason: Headroom on the shared board token is the measure of record and no check may reach the live board or its token, so it is counted at a loopback GitHub endpoint through the real binary.
budgets.workload: A document copy carrying 6 new images, and a task copy carrying 2, into a github-projects source pointed at the loopback endpoint; the repository-id read is counted once per source instance and excluded from the per-image figure. budgets.evidence: Manager's probe, 2026-10-06: one upload (HTTP 201, 0.8 s) plus one authenticated GET (200) per image; no spike.

budgets.name: GitHub copy time for a 24-image plan
budgets.measure: The time, in simulated seconds standing in for the wall time a person waits, of one `onetaskgraph` project copy that a person waits on in `just finish-plan`, for the largest visual plan into a `github-projects` source, with the plugin's default pacing.
budgets.inner_measure_reason: The measure of record is the real copy to the board, which no check may reach. So it is the simulated time of the same copy through the real binary, against a loopback GitHub endpoint that holds each upload's answer for 800 ms of virtual time (the latency the manager measured on 2026-10-06) and each other request's for 200 ms, with the plugin's pacing on the same clock. Simulated rather than real time, so the figure is deterministic, cacheable, and costs no gate time sleeping through pacing.
budgets.workload: One project copy carrying a plan with 7 tasks and 3 documents, two of them holding 12 new images each (24 uploads, 24 verifying reads, about 25 mutations), default pacing (750 ms between content-creating requests). Every image is a PNG generated in the journey of about 500 KB (450,000 to 500,000 bytes), about 12 MB per copy, received in full by the loopback; the journey records each image's size and the analysis fails without a figure when the count or any size differs.
budgets.evidence: Arithmetic: about 49 content-creating requests paced at 750 ms is at least 37 s of simulated time, and the 0.8 s uploads overlap that spacing; manager's probe of 0.8 s per upload. No spike.

budgets.name: GitHub copies refused, 3 at once
budgets.measure: How many of 3 simultaneous project copies of the largest visual plan end refused by a rate limit: the first failure a person sees when several managers finish plans at once.
budgets.inner_measure_reason: GitHub's real secondary limiter cannot be provoked by a check without spending the shared board token's allowance. So 3 concurrent binary processes, attached to one simulated clock, run against a loopback endpoint that enforces GitHub's published secondary limit in virtual time: 80 content-creating requests in any rolling 60 s across all clients, refused past it with the secondary-limit 403 and a `Retry-After`. Virtual time, so the minutes of backoff cost no gate time.
budgets.workload: 3 processes start the same-sized copy within 1 s of each other, each a plan with 24 new images and about 25 mutations (about 147 content-creating requests in all), each with default pacing and retry budget (120 s per call). Each copy's 24 images are generated PNGs of about 500 KB (450,000 to 500,000 bytes), about 36 MB across the three copies; the journey records each image's size and the analysis fails without a figure when the count or any size differs.
budgets.evidence: Arithmetic: 147 requests at 80 a minute drain in about 110 s, and no single call waits more than one 60 s window, which is inside the 120 s retry budget. No spike.

It runs no journey and no `cargo test`, and it is cached on the domain tree, the measured production code and the onebudgetspec pin.

budgets.name: Linear copies refused, 3 at once
budgets.measure: How many of 3 simultaneous project copies of the largest visual plan into a `linear` source, sharing one key, end refused by Linear's rate limit.
budgets.inner_measure_reason: The production key is shared by every manager and no check may spend it. So 3 concurrent binary processes, attached to one simulated clock and sharing one key, run against the loopback workspace enforcing, in virtual time, the per-key request limit Linear publishes, which the node reads from Linear's documentation and records in the budget's description. Past it the workspace refuses with `RATELIMITED` and its reset hint. Virtual time, so the waits cost no gate time.
budgets.workload: 3 processes start the same copy as linear-asset-copy-seconds within 1 s of each other, sharing one key. Each copy's 24 images are generated PNGs of about 500 KB (450,000 to 500,000 bytes), about 36 MB across the three copies; the journey records each image's size and the analysis fails without a figure when the count or any size differs.
budgets.evidence: Design: about 72 asset requests per copy, about 216 across three, waited out within a bounded retry. No spike; the published limit is the node's to read and record.
